The Gospel of John

A visual tour of the Fourth Gospel for A level Religious Studies.

John 20:31

  • ΚΑΤΑ ΙΩΑΝΝΗΝ kata Iōannēn, ‘according to John’ Author and purpose Who wrote the Gospel, when, where and why. The debate, with a map and a timeline. Enter room 1

The Greek above the title is the Gospel’s first line: In the beginning was the Word. Every dotted word in the tour opens its definition, and the glossary lists them all.

Where everything happens in John

John has 21 chapters. This ruler shows the four parts of the Gospel and where each sign and each saying falls. All seven signs sit in the Book of Signs. Five of the seven sayings sit there too, each close to a sign. The last two belong to the Farewell Discourses in the Book of Glory.

How to use the tour

  • Start anywhere. Each room stands on its own, so you can pick up the topic you missed without reading the others first.
  • Gold-lined text is Scripture. It is quoted word for word, with its reference underneath.
  • Dotted words have definitions. Select one to read it, then carry on where you were.
  • Strengths come before weaknesses. Every debate is set out that way so you can weigh a view before you judge it.
  • Each room ends with questions. They are written in Edexcel style. They are not past-paper questions.
  • Need bigger print? The A+ button at the top enlarges the text and opens up the spacing.

Author and purpose

The Fourth Gospel never names its author. It does tell us why it was written. This room sets out the debate about who stands behind the Gospel, when and where it took shape, and what it was written to do.

  • On this page
  • Who wrote it?
  • Scholars compared
  • When?
  • Where?
  • The community
  • Why was it written?
  • John and the Synoptics
  • Questions

What the specification asks (topic 3.2)

  • The different purposes of the Gospel and views of its authorship: Jesus as Christ, Son of God, life in his name; a Spiritual Gospel; a Gospel to convert Jews and Gentiles; fulfilment of scripture.
  • The strengths and weaknesses of these views, based on the text and modern scholarship.
  • Their significance for understanding the text, for individuals and communities.
  • Named scholars: R Brown and C H Dodd.

Who wrote the Gospel?

All four Gospels come to us without an author’s name. The title ‘According to John’ (kata Iōannēn) rests on an early tradition that the apostle John, the son of Zebedee, wrote it. Scholars question that tradition on three grounds.

  1. The external evidence, from early Christian writers, is second-hand and may be confused.
  2. The internal evidence, from the Gospel itself, never names the author.
  3. The content of the Gospel suggests to some scholars that its author was not an eyewitness or one of the Twelve.

External evidence: the tradition about John at Ephesus

The discussion usually starts with Irenaeus (about 130–200 CE). He wrote that John, the disciple of the Lord who leaned on his breast, published the Gospel while living at Ephesus. Irenaeus also says he heard Polycarp (died 155) describe his contact with John and with others who had seen the Lord.

Strengths of the tradition

  • It is the earliest explicit statement that John wrote the Gospel.
  • It claims a short chain of memory: John, then Polycarp, then Irenaeus.
  • It fits the Gospel’s own picture of a disciple leaning against Jesus’ breast (13:23).

Weaknesses of the tradition

  • Other early writing linked with Ephesus, such as the letter of Ignatius to the Ephesians, mentions no ministry of the apostle John there.
  • Irenaeus heard this as a boy, at second hand. Eusebius notes that Papias, whom Irenaeus also calls a hearer of John, said he had heard John the Presbyter, not the apostle. Two men called John may have been confused.
  • Later statements, from Clement of Alexandria and the Muratorian Canon, read like legends shaped to support an apostle as author.

Internal evidence: the disciple whom Jesus loved

The Gospel points to one unnamed figure as its source: the Beloved Disciple. He appears at the Last Supper, at the cross, at the empty tomb and by the lake.

One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was at the table, leaning against Jesus’ breast.

John 13:23

He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. He knows that he tells the truth, that you may believe.

John 19:35

This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. We know that his witness is true.

John 21:24

Two questions follow. Does 21:24 mean the Beloved Disciple wrote the whole Gospel? And can he be identified as John, the son of Zebedee?

Reasons to link the Gospel with an eyewitness

  • The text claims eyewitness testimony for itself, at the cross (19:35) and in its closing lines (21:24).
  • The Beloved Disciple is placed at the key moments, close to Jesus and alongside Peter (13:23–25; 20:3–10; 21:7).
  • C H Dodd showed that John draws on a historical tradition independent of the other Gospels.

Reasons for caution

  • wrote these things can be translated ‘caused these things to be written’. That would make the Beloved Disciple the source, not the writer.
  • We know that his witness is true is another voice speaking about him. It reads like a statement by a church leader vouching for his testimony.
  • The Gospel never names the Beloved Disciple. The sons of Zebedee are mentioned only once (21:2).

Chapter 21: a later ending?

The Gospel seems to finish at 20:30–31. Many scholars treat chapter 21 as an appendix added afterwards, perhaps because eyewitnesses were dying. A saying had spread that the Beloved Disciple would not die, and the chapter corrects it.

This saying therefore went out amongst the brothers that this disciple wouldn’t die. Yet Jesus didn’t say to him that he wouldn’t die, but, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you?”

John 21:23

On the other hand, the language, style and themes of chapter 21 match the rest of the Gospel (Osborne), so the same author may have written both.

A widely held view today

Many scholars now think the Beloved Disciple was a real follower of Jesus, though not one of the Twelve. He gathered a circle of disciples. One or more of them wrote the Gospel, preserving, shaping and interpreting his witness. Raymond Brown called this circle the Johannine community and found several stages of editing in the text.

  1. A witnessThe Beloved Disciple follows Jesus and remembers what he saw.
  2. A circleHe teaches a group of disciples, who preserve and interpret his testimony.
  3. A written GospelOne or more of them write it down, in more than one stage.
  4. A final editionChapter 21 is added, with a note vouching for the witness (21:24).

Strengths of the community view

  • It explains the ‘we’ of 21:24 and the two endings (20:30–31 and 21:24–25).
  • It explains why the vocabulary of the Prologue, such as Logos and ‘grace’, does not return later: parts were composed separately.
  • It keeps a real eyewitness at the root of the tradition.

Weaknesses of the community view

  • The stages are a reconstruction. No earlier edition of the Gospel survives.
  • The even style of the whole Gospel, including chapter 21, makes separate hands hard to prove.
  • It sets aside the only early tradition we have, which names John.

Scholars compared

Views on authorship and date
ScholarWho wrote it?DateWhy it matters
Irenaeus (about 130–200 CE)The apostle John, son of Zebedee, at EphesusLate first centuryThe earliest explicit claim that John wrote it. It depends on second-hand tradition through Polycarp.
C H DoddAnonymous. The tradition is independent of the SynopticsAbout 90–100 CENamed the Book of Signs and Book of Glory. Showed that John uses independent historical tradition.
Raymond BrownThe Beloved Disciple is the founding witness. His disciples wrote the final textAbout 90–100 CEProposed the Johannine community and several stages of editing.
C K BarrettNot the apostle. Anonymous, or the work of a communityAbout 90–100 CEArgued for a Gospel written after the Synoptics, with developed theology.
R SchnackenburgNot the apostle. The tradition is rooted in the Beloved DiscipleAbout 90–100 CESeparated the Beloved Disciple’s witness from later editorial work.
J A T RobinsonThe apostle John as the primary witnessAbout 50–65 CEArgued for the ‘priority of John’: the Synoptics are not always the historical baseline.

Key points: authorship

  • The Gospel is anonymous. The name ‘John’ comes from tradition (Irenaeus).
  • The text points to the Beloved Disciple as its witness (19:35; 21:24).
  • ‘Wrote’ in 21:24 may mean ‘caused to be written’.
  • Brown: an eyewitness, a community, and more than one edition.
  • Why it matters: an eyewitness source supports the Gospel’s historical value. A community source explains its developed theology. The Gospel itself presents its content as testimony written to produce belief.

When was it written?

Older scholarship put John in the second century, because its theology looked developed and it was thought to depend on the Synoptic Gospels. One small piece of papyrus changed that. The Rylands Papyrus P52, found in Egypt and dated to the early second century, contains lines from John 18. A copy was already in Egypt by then, so the Gospel itself must be earlier.

  1. About 28–30 CEJesus is executed by order of Pilate.
  2. About 50–65 CERobinson’s early date. The Gospel reaches its final form before the Jewish war with Rome.
  3. 70 CEThe Temple in Jerusalem is destroyed.
  4. About 85–90 CEThe council at Jamnia and the Birkat ha-minim, which some link to believers being put out of the synagogue.
  5. About 90–100 CEThe date most scholars accept (Brown, Schnackenburg, Barrett).
  6. Early second centuryThe Rylands Papyrus P52 is copied in Egypt. This sets the latest possible date, the terminus ante quem.
  7. After 100 CEThe older view, now largely abandoned.
Three views on the date
ViewDateHeld byMain evidence
EarlyAbout 50–65 CEJ A T RobinsonJohn is an independent, primary source for the historical Jesus. Its final form comes before the war of 66–70.
StandardAbout 90–100 CEBrown, Schnackenburg, BarrettP52 sets the latest date. Developed Christology and the references to expulsion from the synagogue suggest the late first century.
Second centuryAfter 100 CEOlder liberal scholarshipAssumed dependence on the Synoptics and very developed theology. Largely abandoned after P52.

Most scholars have not followed Robinson all the way. His work did reopen the question of whether John belongs early or late within the years 70–100.

Where was it written?

  • AEphesus. The traditional place of publication, according to Irenaeus.
  • BHierapolis. Home of Papias, who said he had heard John the Presbyter.
  • CAntioch in Syria. A major early Christian centre, also proposed as the place of writing.
  • DAlexandria. Another proposal. It was the city of Philo of Alexandria, and P52 was found in Egypt.
  • EJerusalem and Palestine. Some scholars think the traditions began here and were shaped into their final form in a Diaspora setting, where Greek religious ideas were stronger.

The community behind the Gospel

Clues in the text suggest a community under pressure. The Gospel often sets ‘the Jews’ as a group over against those who believe in Jesus. This reflects tension between church and synagogue. Three times it speaks of believers being put out of the synagogue.

His parents said these things because they feared the Jews; for the Jews had already agreed that if any man would confess him as Christ, he would be put out of the synagogue.

John 9:22

They will put you out of the synagogues. Yes, the time is coming that whoever kills you will think that he offers service to God.

John 16:2

Some scholars link this with the Birkat ha-minim issued at Jamnia around 85–90 CE. The link is debated. Chapters 14–17 then speak to the community’s own life: the role of the Holy Spirit, the need for love and unity, the threat of persecution, and its mission in the world. The community probably included both Jewish and Gentile Christians.

Why was the Gospel written?

John is the only Gospel that states its purpose in so many words.

Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

John 20:30–31

This one sentence holds several aims. The specification names four. Scholars have suggested others.

1. Jesus as Christ, Son of God, life in his name

The purpose is belief, and the result of belief is life. Martha’s confession before the raising of Lazarus uses almost the same words as 20:31:

I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son, he who comes into the world.

John 11:27

Was John written to win new believers or to strengthen existing ones? Manuscripts differ over the tense of ‘believe’ in 20:31, so the verse can be read either way. The Gospel as a whole does both.

2. A spiritual Gospel

Clement of Alexandria said that John wrote a ‘spiritual Gospel’ while the others recorded the ‘bodily facts’. This was the first attempt to explain why John is so different. On this view John’s aim is to bring out the inner meaning of Jesus’ life.

Strength: it fits John’s long discourses and his symbols. Weakness: it can suggest John is not interested in history, yet Dodd and Robinson argue that he preserves early, independent tradition.

3. A Gospel to convert Jews and Gentiles

John explains how Jesus relates to Judaism, and he makes room for Gentile believers:

I have other sheep which are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice. They will become one flock with one shepherd.

John 10:16

He gives the title Messiah in both its Semitic and its Greek form (1:41; 4:25). His opening uses Logos, a word Greek thinkers knew well. Dodd argued that John presents the Gospel in terms an educated Greek-speaking reader could follow.

4. Fulfilment of scripture

John shows Jesus fulfilling the Scriptures of Israel. He is greater than Abraham and Moses (8:58; 1:17), and he fulfils and replaces the feasts and institutions of Judaism (Brown). When Jesus rides into Jerusalem, John quotes the prophet Zechariah:

Jesus, having found a young donkey, sat on it. As it is written, “Don’t be afraid, daughter of Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting on a donkey’s colt.”

John 12:14–15

The disciples only understood this later, when Jesus was glorified (12:16).

Other purposes scholars have proposed

Further aims, with the evidence for each
PurposeEvidence in the textHow strong is it?
To encourage later believers who never saw the signsBlessed are those who have not seen and have believed (20:29)Strong. It stands right beside the purpose statement.
To support a community put out of the synagogue9:22; 12:42; 16:2Strong on the tension. The link to the Birkat ha-minim is debated.
To set John the Baptist in his proper placeHe was not the light (1:8). Compare Acts 19:1–7, where some know only the Baptist’s baptism.Plausible. The Gospel honours the Baptist as a witness but keeps him below Jesus.
To defend the Beloved Disciple’s authority beside PeterThe two run to the tomb together (20:3–10). Chapter 21 gives each his own calling.Weaker. Peter is shown positively throughout, so a rivalry inside the community is doubtful.
To oppose DocetismThe Word became flesh (1:14); 6:51–58Plausible. The flesh of Jesus is stressed at key points.

Weighing the purposes

Why 20:31 should lead

  • It is the author’s own statement, placed at the climax of the Gospel.
  • It matches what the Gospel does throughout: signs, sayings and confessions all push the reader to decide who Jesus is.
  • The other purposes fit inside it. A community under pressure, later believers and Gentile readers all need the same thing: grounds for belief.

Why 20:31 is not the whole story

  • It is a broad statement. It does not say who the readers were or what they faced.
  • If the Gospel grew in stages, different stages may have had different aims.
  • Chapter 21 adds concerns of its own: Peter, the Beloved Disciple and the mission of the church.

Key points: purpose

  • Learn 20:31. It names the titles Christ and Son of God and the goal, life.
  • The four purposes in the specification are not rivals. They overlap.
  • For individuals, the purpose is personal belief. For communities, it is identity: who belongs to God’s people, and on what basis.

John and the Synoptic Gospels

The authorship debate matters because John is so different from Matthew, Mark and Luke.

What John leaves out, and what only John has
Not found in JohnFound only in John
ParablesJesus’ early ministry of baptising by the Jordan
Exorcisms and the healing of lepersThe meetings with Nicodemus and the Samaritan woman
The infancy stories, the Temptation and the TransfigurationThe long ‘I am’ discourses
Table fellowship with sinners; the SadduceesMost of chapters 7–11 and 14–17
The institution of the Lord’s SupperThe footwashing, and the conversation with Pilate

Of the signs in John, only the feeding of the five thousand appears in the Synoptics. Most scholars no longer think John depends on them. They see him drawing on an independent tradition with historical value. Robinson went furthest: John’s witness should stand beside the Synoptic picture and sometimes correct it.

The Prologue

John opens with eighteen verses unlike anything else in the Gospels. They say who Jesus is before the story starts. This room gives you the text, the debate about what kind of writing it is and what it is for, and the argument over where its ideas come from.

  • On this page
  • The text
  • What kind of text?
  • What is it for?
  • Gnostic, Greek, Jewish or Essene?
  • What it means
  • Codes for living
  • In the exam

What the specification asks (topic 2.1)

  • The meaning and theological significance of the Prologue: the nature and person of Jesus, the Word made flesh, and the concepts of life, light and dark, belief, children of God, flesh and spirit, law, grace and truth.
  • The influences of Judaism and Hellenism, and why they matter for understanding the Gospel.
  • The implications for religious laws and codes for living of different understandings of who Jesus is.
  • Named scholars: C H Dodd and M Hooker. The Prologue is Extract 2 in the anthology.

The text: John 1:1–18

Read it through once before anything else. The verses fall into four movements. The tinted rows are about John the Baptist. Many scholars think they were added to an older poem.

John 1:1–18, World English Bible British Edition. Tinted rows are the verses about John the Baptist.
Verses 1–5: The Word before creation
1In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
2The same was in the beginning with God.
3All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.
4In him was life, and the life was the light of men.
5The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.
Verses 6–8: The witness
6There came a man sent from God, whose name was John.
7The same came as a witness, that he might testify about the light, that all might believe through him.
8He was not the light, but was sent that he might testify about the light.
Verses 9–13: The Word comes into the world
9The true light that enlightens everyone was coming into the world.
10He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world didn’t recognise him.
11He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him.
12But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name:
13who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
Verses 14–18: The Word made flesh
14The Word became flesh and lived amongst us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.
15John testified about him. He cried out, saying, “This was he of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me has surpassed me, for he was before me.’”
16From his fullness we all received grace upon grace.
17For the law was given through Moses. Grace and truth were realised through Jesus Christ.
18No one has seen God at any time. The only born Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him.
The four movements
VersesMovementKey idea
1–5The Word before creationThe Word is eternal and divine, and is the source of creation, life and light.
6–8The witnessJohn the Baptist points to the light. He is not the light.
9–13The Word comes into the worldHis own reject him. Those who believe become children of God.
14–18The Word made fleshThe incarnation: glory, grace and truth. Jesus makes the unseen God known.

Four words to learn first

  • Logos: the Greek word translated ‘Word’. It can also mean speech, reason or rational principle.
  • Pre-existence: the Word existed before creation (verses 1–2).
  • Incarnation: God becoming human, the claim of verse 14.
  • lived amongst us (verse 14): the Greek verb, eskēnōsen, literally means ‘pitched his tent’. It recalls the Tabernacle in the wilderness. The NIV in your anthology has ‘made his dwelling’.

What kind of text is it?

Scholars disagree about what the Prologue is and when it was written. The answer affects how much weight it carries when you interpret the rest of the Gospel. There are five main theories. They are not always rivals.

Theory A: an early Christian hymn

  • The Prologue is poetic and rhythmic, unlike the prose that follows.
  • It uses staircase parallelism: Word, Word, God in verse 1; life, light, darkness in verses 4–5.
  • The Baptist verses (6–8 and 15) interrupt the flow, as if prose had been inserted into a poem.
  • Key words such as Logos, grace and fullness never return in the Gospel with these meanings.
  • Raymond Brown argued that it was an early Christian hymn, adapted to introduce the Gospel. C K Barrett saw it as focused on explaining Jesus’ divinity. Rudolf Bultmann went further and argued that the hymn was older than Christianity and came from Gnostic circles.

Strength

It explains the change of style and the awkward position of the Baptist verses.

Weakness

No copy of an original hymn exists, and scholars cannot agree which verses belonged to it.

Theory B: a later addition

  • J A T Robinson argued that the author added the Prologue after the Gospel was written, to help the early Church understand Jesus. It was not originally a hymn or a prayer.
  • Brown also thought the hymn was attached at a late stage of editing.
  • The Gospel reads naturally if it starts at 1:19 with the Baptist’s testimony, much as Mark begins.

Strength

It accounts for the vocabulary that never returns, and for the smooth start at 1:19.

Weakness

If Robinson is right, the links between the Prologue and the Gospel might be coincidence. Yet an author who adds an introduction later still chooses it to fit the whole work.

Theory C: an overture, the key to the Gospel

Morna Hooker sees the Prologue as the key that unlocks the Fourth Gospel. Each Gospel, she argues, begins by giving readers information the characters in the story do not have. Like the overture to an opera, the Prologue introduces the themes to come.

Themes the Prologue announces, and where they return
In the PrologueLater in the Gospel
the Word was God (1:1)Thomas: My Lord and my God! (20:28). The two verses frame the whole Gospel.
Light and darkness (1:4–5)I am the light of the world (8:12), and the healing of the man born blind (John 9)
In him was life (1:4)I am the bread of life (6:35), and the purpose of the Gospel (20:31)
those who were his own didn’t receive him (1:11)The conflicts of chapters 8 and 10
We saw his glory (1:14)The first sign at Cana revealed his glory (2:11)
Belief (1:7, 12)that you may believe (20:31)

Strength

The links are clear and numerous. Whatever its origin, the Prologue works as a key for readers.

Weakness

This is about what the Prologue does. It does not settle where it came from.

Theory D: a Jewish-style commentary on Genesis

The first words echo the first words of the Bible. Some scholars read the Prologue as a midrash on Genesis 1:1–5, which has the same sequence: beginning, creation, light, darkness.

In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.

Genesis 1:1

God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.

Genesis 1:3

On this reading the Prologue tells of a new creation. In Jesus, God begins creation afresh.

Theory E: a mirror structure

A chiasm puts its most important point in the centre. R Alan Culpepper argued that the Prologue is built this way. The Word with God (verse 1) mirrors the Son close to the Father (verse 18). The Baptist’s witness (verses 6–8) mirrors his witness in verse 15. The centre is verses 12–13.

But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name…

John 1:12

Strength

It makes salvation and belief the heart of the Prologue, alongside Christology.

Weakness

Critics say a chiasm can be found in many texts if you look hard enough.

Key points: what kind of text?

  • Hymn: Brown and Barrett. Bultmann’s version is pre-Christian and Gnostic.
  • Later addition: Robinson.
  • Key or overture: Hooker.
  • Midrash on Genesis 1: a new creation.
  • Chiasm: Culpepper, centred on verses 12–13.
  • The best answers weigh these views. A hymn could be added later and work as a key.

What is the Prologue for?

Whatever its origin, the Prologue does several jobs at the head of the Gospel. Scholars stress different ones.

Suggested purposes of the Prologue
PurposeHow the text supports itWho stresses it
To hand the reader the keyThe reader learns at once that the Word was God and became flesh. The characters in the story have to work this out.Hooker
To explain Jesus’ divinityVerses 1–3 and 18 place the Word with God before creation.Barrett
To guide the early ChurchAn introduction written last, to help believers read the Gospel rightly.Robinson
To put John the Baptist in his placeHe was not the light (1:8). This may correct followers who valued the Baptist too highly (compare Acts 19:1–7).Seen in verses 6–8 and 15
To set Jesus beside Mosesthe law was given through Moses; grace and truth come through Jesus Christ (1:17).Brown: verses 14–18 preview John’s replacement theology
To prepare for belief and unbeliefSome do not receive him (1:11). Others receive him and believe (1:12). The rest of the Gospel sorts people the same way.Seen in verses 10–13
To insist that Jesus was truly humanThe Word became flesh rules out Docetism.Seen in verse 14
To speak to Jews and Greeks at once‘Word’ would call to mind both the Jewish Scriptures and Greek philosophy.Dodd

Gnostic, Greek, Jewish or Essene?

John wrote in a world where Jewish and Greek ideas mixed. Scholars debate which background best explains the Prologue. The specification names two: Judaism and Hellenism. The Gnostic and Essene cases sharpen the argument.

Is it Gnostic?

Gnosticism taught that salvation comes through secret knowledge and that matter is inferior or evil.

The case

  • Bultmann argued that the original hymn was pre-Christian and Gnostic, and that Christians adapted it.
  • He linked the Prologue with Gnostic ideas of a heavenly redeemer.
  • Before 1947 many scholars assumed that John’s language of light and darkness must be Greek or Gnostic.

The problems

  • Most scholars now think this goes beyond the evidence. No such hymn has been found.
  • For Gnostics matter was evil. A Word who became flesh is the opposite of Gnostic teaching.
  • The Dead Sea Scrolls show that the same dualism already existed inside Judaism (Brown).

Verdict: the weakest of the four cases.

Is it Greek?

Educated readers across the Roman Empire, including many Jews, knew Greek philosophy.

The case

  • Heraclitus (about 500 BCE): the Logos is the rational principle that orders the universe. Compare verse 3.
  • The Stoics: the Logos is divine reason in all things, and every person shares a seed of it. Compare The true light that enlightens everyone (1:9).
  • Plato: a contrast between the perfect unseen world and the changing material world. Compare light and darkness, flesh and spirit.
  • Philo of Alexandria: the Logos is God’s intermediary in creation, even God’s firstborn. This is the closest parallel.
  • Dodd took this background seriously: John writes so that an educated Greek-speaking reader can understand.

The problems

  • Verse 14 would shock a Greek philosopher. For Plato and the Stoics the divine Logos would never become flesh.
  • Philo’s Logos is never a person who lives a human life.

Verdict: Greek language, but not a Greek message.

Is it Jewish?

The Prologue is full of the Jewish Scriptures.

The case

  • God’s word creates. In the Old Testament God’s word is active and makes things happen (see the quotations below).
  • Memra. The Targums use ‘Word’ as a respectful way to speak of God acting in the world.
  • Torah. Dodd suggested that God’s Word would be identified with the Law. That gives verse 17 its force.
  • Wisdom. In the Wisdom literature, Wisdom is with God at creation, comes to live in Israel and is rejected. The Prologue follows the same pattern.
  • Tabernacle and glory. Verse 14 echoes God’s presence, the Shekinah, filling the Tabernacle.

The problems

  • Wisdom is a personification, a poetic figure. John’s Word is a real person who becomes human.
  • John chose Logos, not Sophia. Perhaps this is because Jesus was male, or because Logos spoke to Jews and Greeks alike.

Verdict: the strongest case, with detailed parallels.

Is it Essene?

The Essenes were a strict Jewish group. Most scholars link them with Qumran and the Dead Sea Scrolls, found from 1947 onwards.

The case

  • Light and darkness. The Community Rule describes two spirits, of truth and of falsehood, and calls people ‘sons of light’ or ‘sons of darkness’. The War Scroll describes a final battle between them.
  • Truth. The scrolls speak often of ‘truth’ and ‘the spirit of truth’. Compare full of grace and truth (1:14).
  • Everything comes from God. A hymn at the end of the Community Rule says nothing happens apart from God. Compare verse 3.
  • The wilderness. The Qumran community and John the Baptist both applied Isaiah 40:3 to themselves.
  • Brown argued that the scrolls show such ideas already existed within Palestinian Judaism.

The problems

  • Qumran’s dualism is exclusive: light belongs to the chosen community. John’s light is for everyone (1:9), and anyone who believes can become a child of God (1:12).
  • Qumran has no idea of a Word becoming flesh.
  • Any direct contact between the Baptist and Qumran cannot be proved.

Verdict: strong support for a Jewish background, but not the source.

The Jewish evidence in the text

God’s word at work in creation and history:

By the LORD’s word, the heavens were made: all their army by the breath of his mouth.

Psalm 33:6

So is my word that goes out of my mouth: it will not return to me void, but it will accomplish that which I please.

Isaiah 55:11

The voice in the wilderness that both Qumran and the Baptist claimed:

The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of the LORD in the wilderness!”

Isaiah 40:3
Wisdom and the Word side by side
Wisdom textWhat it says about WisdomParallel in the Prologue
Proverbs 8:22–23The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his work … from the beginning, before the earth existedIn the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God (1:1)
Proverbs 8:30then I was the craftsman by his sideAll things were made through him (1:3)
Wisdom of Solomon 7:26she is a reflection of everlasting lightThe true light (1:9)
Wisdom of Solomon 9:1God made all things by your wordAll things were made through him (1:3)
Sirach 24:8He who created me made my tent to restlived amongst us, literally ‘pitched his tent’ (1:14)
Sirach 24:23Wisdom is the law which Moses commanded usthe law was given through Moses. Grace and truth were realised through Jesus Christ (1:17)
Proverbs 1; SirachWisdom is often rejected by people.those who were his own didn’t receive him (1:11)

The Tabernacle, God’s character and the limit placed on Moses all stand behind verses 14–18:

Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and the LORD’s glory filled the tabernacle.

Exodus 40:34

The LORD! The LORD, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth

Exodus 34:6

He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”

Exodus 33:20

Moses could not see God’s face. John says that the only Son has made God known (1:18).

Putting the influences together

Greek thought

Logos as divine reason. Philo’s Logos as God’s agent.

Word and Torah

God’s creating word. Memra. The Law given through Moses.

Jewish Wisdom

With God at creation. Tents in Israel. Rejected.

Essene language

Light against darkness. Truth. All things from God.

What John does with them

The 2023 Edexcel mark scheme credits the view, linked with Marsh, that the author used every tool at his disposal. It is no surprise to find Old Testament, rabbinic and Stoic ideas together. Then John says what none of these sources says: The Word became flesh.

Key points: influences

  • Gnostic (Bultmann): now doubted. Flesh is the problem.
  • Greek (Heraclitus, Stoics, Philo; Dodd): explains the word Logos, but no Greek thinker says the Logos became flesh.
  • Jewish (Wisdom, Word, Torah, Tabernacle): the closest match to the Prologue’s pattern.
  • Essene (Dead Sea Scrolls; Brown): shows that the light and darkness language is Jewish, but Qumran’s light is for the few.
  • Best judgement: John draws on several backgrounds and transforms them all with verse 14.

What the Prologue means

Each concept below is named in the specification. Use the table for AO1 on meaning and significance.

The theology of the Prologue
ConceptVersesMeaningWhy it matters in John
The nature and person of Jesus1–2, 18The Word is eternal. He is distinct from God (with God) and yet divine (was God).John has the highest Christology of the four Gospels. Later it informs the doctrine of the Trinity.
The Word made flesh14God truly becomes a human being.It rejects the idea that Jesus only seemed human. The Word can be seen, heard and touched.
Creation3, 10All things were made through the Word.Jesus is not a created being. The world belongs to him even when it rejects him.
Life4The Word is the source of all life, physical and spiritual.It prepares for eternal life and for the signs, above all the raising of Lazarus.
Light and dark4–5, 9Light is God’s truth and presence. Darkness is ignorance, sin and opposition.the darkness hasn’t overcome it: a hint of victory at the cross. It links to 8:12 and John 9.
Belief7, 12To believe in his name is to trust who Jesus is.Belief is the Gospel’s whole purpose (20:31). People in the story are judged by their response.
Children of God12–13Believers are born of God, not by physical descent.Belonging depends on faith, not ethnic origin, so it is open to Jews and Gentiles. It links to being born anew in John 3.
Flesh and spirit13–14‘Flesh’ is human life. Spiritual birth comes from God.Human effort cannot create a relationship with God. God enters flesh to make it possible.
Law, grace and truth14, 16–17The Law, through Moses, was a gift. Jesus brings the fullness of grace and truth.It supports the view that Jesus fulfils and surpasses the Law and Moses.
Glory and revelation14, 18God’s glory, once in the Tabernacle, is now seen in Jesus, who makes the unseen God known.Jesus is the full revelation of God. His glory shows in the signs and finally at the cross.
Witness6–8, 15John the Baptist testifies. He is less than Jesus.Witness is a key theme of the Gospel.
Rejection10–11The world and his own fail to recognise him.It foreshadows the conflict and the crucifixion.

Key points: meaning

  • Verse 1: the Word is eternal and divine. Verse 14: the Word becomes fully human. Hold both together.
  • The Prologue introduces the Gospel’s big themes: life, light, belief, glory, truth, rejection.
  • Salvation is becoming children of God through belief (verses 12–13).
  • Jesus fulfils and surpasses the Law, Moses and the Tabernacle (verses 14–18).

Religious laws and codes for living

  • If Jesus is the Word made flesh, his teaching carries God’s authority, above the Law given through Moses (1:17). This underpins Christian ethics built on Jesus’ command to love (John 15).
  • If anyone who believes can become a child of God (1:12), religious identity does not rest on birth, food laws or ritual. That helped Christianity spread beyond Judaism.
  • The idea of a light that enlightens everyone (1:9) has been used to argue that all people share a God-given capacity for truth and moral understanding.

A caution about ‘replacement’

A replacement reading has sometimes fed hostility towards Judaism. Many modern scholars stress that John also presents the Law as a real gift: the NIV in your anthology speaks of ‘grace in place of grace’ in verse 16.

Using the Prologue in the exam

  • AO1: give precise verse references, accurate terms (Logos, incarnation, Wisdom, midrash, dualism) and named scholars.
  • AO2: weigh the views. The 2023 mark scheme rewarded answers that set Hooker against Robinson, and that used Brown and Dodd to argue for the weight of Jewish influences.
  • The anthology passage may be printed on the paper. Quote short phrases from it and analyse them.

A plan to adapt: ‘The Prologue is best understood against a Greek background.’ Evaluate.

SectionWhat to write
IntroductionDefine Logos and Hellenism. State your judgement: the language is Greek, but the meaning is mainly Jewish.
Paragraph 1For: Heraclitus, the Stoics, Philo. Dodd on Greek-speaking readers. Verse 9, light for everyone. Give a mini-judgement.
Paragraph 2Against: the Wisdom parallels (Proverbs 8, Sirach 24). Genesis 1. Dodd on Torah. Give a mini-judgement.
Paragraph 3Against: the Dead Sea Scrolls show that light and darkness language is Jewish (Brown). Note the limits of the Qumran parallel.
Paragraph 4Verse 14 breaks with both Greek thought and Wisdom. Something new is being said. Marsh: John used every tool available.
ConclusionReturn to your judgement: a Jewish core, expressed in language Greeks could understand.

Sentence starters for evaluation

  • ‘Hooker’s view is strengthened by the number of themes that return later, such as…’
  • ‘Robinson’s argument challenges this, because if the Prologue was added later…’
  • ‘The Hellenistic reading struggles to explain verse 14, since…’
  • ‘The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls weakens the claim that… because…’
  • ‘Therefore the most convincing view is that John combines… because…’

‘I am’ sayings and the Book of Signs

In John, Jesus does seven signs and says ‘I am’ in a way no other Gospel records. The two belong together. A sign shows who Jesus is. A saying tells you what the sign means.

  • On this page
  • What ‘I am’ means
  • What a sign is
  • Map
  • Signs and sayings paired
  • The seven signs
  • Way and vine
  • ‘I am’ alone
  • Big ideas and scholars
  • Debates
  • Questions

What the specification asks (topics 2.2 and 2.3)

  • 2.2 The meaning and significance of ‘I am the bread of life’, ‘the light of the world’, ‘the good shepherd’ and ‘the true vine’. Their background and context, including Old Testament references and symbolism.
  • 2.3 The meaning and significance of the seven signs: turning water into wine, the healing of the official’s son, the healing at the pool, the feeding of the 5000, walking on water, the healing of the blind man and the raising of Lazarus. What they show about the identity and role of Jesus.
  • For both: the implications for religious laws and codes for living.
  • Named scholars: R Brown and C H Dodd. Extract 3 in the anthology prints John 6:24–59, 8:12, 9:1–12, 10:1–21 and 15:1–17.

What does ‘I am’ mean?

The Greek is egō eimi. It is ordinary Greek for ‘I am’. In the Greek Old Testament, though, it is how God speaks of himself.

God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

Exodus 3:14

“You are my witnesses,” says the LORD … “that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he.”

Isaiah 43:10

In Isaiah 40–55 ‘I am he’ is God’s repeated claim to be the only God and saviour. So when Jesus says ‘I am’, above all with no noun after it, Jewish hearers could hear a claim to share God’s identity. That is why they reach for stones in 8:59.

Two kinds of ‘I am’ saying
KindWhat it looks likeExamples
Predicated: with a noun‘I am the …’ An image explains what Jesus does for people.Bread of life (6:35). Light of the world (8:12). Door (10:7). Good shepherd (10:11). Resurrection and the life (11:25). Way, truth and life (14:6). True vine (15:1).
Absolute: no noun‘I am’ on its own. A claim about who Jesus is, echoing God’s name.before Abraham came into existence, I AM (8:58). unless you believe that I am he (8:24). I am he at the arrest (18:5–6).

Why the images matter

  • Each image (bread, light, shepherd, vine) was already used in the Old Testament for God or for Israel. Jesus takes a picture of what God gives and says that he is that gift.
  • Several sayings are attached to a sign or to a Jewish festival, so the saying explains the event.
  • Most sayings end with a promise for ‘whoever’ believes. They are invitations as well as claims.

The pattern to remember

Old Testament image, then a festival or a sign, then Jesus fulfils and replaces it, then a promise to whoever believes.

What is a sign?

The Synoptic Gospels call Jesus’ miracles ‘mighty deeds’. John calls them signs (sēmeia). A sign is a revealing act. It points beyond itself to who Jesus is: God’s agent of salvation. You have understood a sign when you see God’s life-giving power at work through Jesus.

Seeing a sign does not guarantee faith.

But though he had done so many signs before them, yet they didn’t believe in him…

John 12:37

John tells us that he chose which signs to record, and why: so that readers may believe (20:30–31).

Sign, then discourse

C H Dodd showed that John’s pattern is a sign followed by a discourse. The event comes first. Then Jesus, or the argument it provokes, explains it. Dodd named chapters 1:19 to 12:50 the Book of Signs.

Signs and festivals

The Book of Signs is organised around the Jewish calendar. Each feast gives a symbolic backdrop for what Jesus does and says. Raymond Brown stressed that Jesus fulfils and replaces the feasts and institutions of Judaism. This is often called replacement theology.

The festivals behind the signs and sayings
Festival or dayIn JohnSign or saying set thereWhat Jesus offers in its place
Sabbath5:9; 9:14The healing at the pool. The healing of the man born blind.The Son works as the Father works and gives life.
Passover6:4The feeding of the five thousand. ‘I am the bread of life.’Bread greater than the manna of Moses.
Tabernacles7:2; 8:12‘I am the light of the world.’The light the festival lamps pointed to.
Dedication10:22–30The shepherd theme returns.The shepherd whose sheep hear his voice: I and the Father are one.

Where the signs happen

  • 1Cana in Galilee. Water becomes wine at a wedding (2:1–11).
  • 2Cana to Capernaum. Jesus speaks at Cana and the official’s son is healed at Capernaum (4:46–54).
  • 3Jerusalem. A man is healed at the pool on the Sabbath (5:1–9).
  • 4The far side of the Sea of Galilee. Five thousand are fed (6:1–15).
  • 5On the Sea of Galilee. Jesus walks on the water (6:16–21).
  • 6Jerusalem. A man born blind washes in the pool of Siloam and sees (9:1–41).
  • 7Bethany. Lazarus is raised (11:1–44).

Also marked: Sychar in Samaria, where Jesus meets the woman at the well (John 4). Qumran, linked with the Essenes and the Dead Sea Scrolls. Jamnia, linked with the Birkat ha-minim. Caesarea, where the Roman prefect lived.

Signs and sayings paired

Four of the seven signs have an ‘I am’ saying tied to them. Three do not. Where there is no saying, the table gives the sign’s key word.

Each sign, the saying tied to it, and what it says about Jesus
SignSaying tied to itWhat it says about Jesus
1. Water into wine (2:1–11)No saying Key word: glory (2:11)He brings the new age and reveals his glory.
2. The official’s son (4:46–54)No saying Key word: life (4:50)His word gives life, even at a distance.
3. The healing at the pool (5:1–9)No saying Key word: work (5:17)He does on the Sabbath what only God may do.
4. Feeding the five thousand (6:1–15)I am the bread of life (6:35)He is the true bread from heaven, greater than the manna of Moses.
5. Walking on water (6:16–21)It is I literally ‘I am’ (6:20)He masters the sea as God does.
6. The man born blind (9:1–41)I am the light of the world (8:12; 9:5)He reveals God, and his coming is a judgement.
7. The raising of Lazarus (11:1–44)I am the resurrection and the life (11:25)He gives life as the Father gives life.

Three sayings have no sign of their own. The door and the good shepherd follow straight on from sign 6. The way and the true vine belong to the Farewell Discourses.

The seven signs, one by one

1

Water into wine

John 2:1–11. A wedding at Cana in Galilee.

The wine runs out at a wedding. Six stone water jars stand ready for washing. Jesus has them filled with water, and what the man in charge of the feast tastes is wine.

Now there were six water pots of stone set there after the Jews’ way of purifying

John 2:6

This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.

John 2:11
Saying tied to it
No ‘I am’ saying The sign is tied to the Prologue. We saw his glory (1:14) becomes revealed his glory (2:11).
What it says about Jesus
He brings the abundance of the messianic age. Water kept for Jewish purification becomes the wine of the new age. The man in charge of the feast says, You have kept the good wine until now!
Response
his disciples believed in him. The first sign does what 20:31 says signs are for.
Scholar
Brown: an example of Jesus fulfilling and replacing a Jewish institution.
2

The healing of the official’s son

John 4:46–54. Jesus is at Cana. The boy is at Capernaum.

An official begs Jesus to come before his child dies. Jesus does not go. He sends the father home with a sentence, and the father believes it before he sees anything.

Jesus said to him, “Go your way. Your son lives.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him, and he went his way.

John 4:50

So the father knew that it was at that hour in which Jesus said to him, “Your son lives.” He believed, as did his whole house.

John 4:53
Saying tied to it
No ‘I am’ saying The key word is life: Your son lives. Compare I am the resurrection and the life (11:25).
What it says about Jesus
His life-giving power is not limited by distance. His word is enough.
Response
The father trusts the word alone. This is the faith the Gospel praises at its close: Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed (20:29).
A warning
Unless you see signs and wonders, you will in no way believe (4:48). Faith that only wants wonders has missed the sign.
3

The healing at the pool

John 5:1–9. The pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem, on a Sabbath.

A man has been ill for thirty-eight years. Jesus heals him with a command. Then John adds the detail that starts the argument.

Jesus said to him, “Arise, take up your mat, and walk.” Immediately, the man was made well, and took up his mat and walked. Now that day was a Sabbath.

John 5:8–9

But Jesus answered them, “My Father is still working, so I am working, too.” For this cause therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God.

John 5:17–18
Saying tied to it
No ‘I am’ saying The key word is work. The discourse that follows (5:19–30) makes the claim openly.
What it says about Jesus
He uses rights that Jewish thought kept for God alone: working on the Sabbath, giving life and judging. as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son also gives life (5:21).
Response
Division. His opponents see exactly what is being claimed: making himself equal with God.
Idea to use
Agency: Jesus acts as God’s authorised agent, so what he does, God does.
4

The feeding of the five thousand

John 6:1–15. The far side of the Sea of Galilee, near Passover.

Jesus feeds a great crowd from five barley loaves and two fish. The crowd call him the prophet and want to make him king, and he withdraws. Next day they come looking for more bread.

When therefore the people saw the sign which Jesus did, they said, “This is truly the prophet who comes into the world.”

John 6:14

Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.”

John 6:26

The saying that explains the sign

Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.”

John 6:35

“I am the living bread which came down out of heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. Yes, the bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”

John 6:51
Saying tied to it
I am the bread of life 6:35, 48, 51. The crowd read the sign as a free meal. The saying tells them what it meant.
Old Testament background
The manna: I will rain bread from the sky for you (Exodus 16:4). Wisdom’s invitation: Come, eat some of my bread (Proverbs 9:5). Compare Isaiah 55:1. Jewish teachers also spoke of the Torah as bread.
What it says about Jesus
  • Greater than Moses. it wasn’t Moses who gave you the bread out of heaven (6:32). Those who ate manna died. Whoever eats this bread will live for ever (6:58).
  • Life now. he who believes in me has eternal life (6:47). This is realised eschatology. The future is kept too: I will raise him up at the last day (6:40).
  • The cross. The bread is my flesh, given for the life of the world. Life comes through his death.
Response
Grumbling (6:41), argument (6:52), and then many of his disciples went back and walked no more with him (6:66). The saying forces a decision.
Scholars
Brown: Jesus replaces the manna, and 6:51–58 is John’s teaching on the Eucharist. Dodd: Jesus takes the place of the Torah as true nourishment.

Debate: is John 6 about the Eucharist?

Jesus therefore said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you don’t have life in yourselves.”

John 6:53

The case that it is

  • The language of 6:53–56 is strikingly physical: flesh and blood, eating and drinking.
  • John has no account of the Lord’s Supper being instituted at the Last Supper. Brown argues that John places his eucharistic teaching here, at Passover.
  • lives in me, and I in him matches early Christian understanding of communion.

The case against

  • The discourse starts with coming and believing, not eating: 6:35.
  • Dodd and others read the bread as Jesus himself, received by faith, in the tradition of Wisdom’s bread and the Torah as food.
  • The flesh profits nothing (6:63). A purely sacramental reading struggles with this verse.

A judgement you could defend: the discourse is mainly about believing in Jesus as the source of eternal life, and the Eucharist is one way that believing is expressed.

5

Walking on water

John 6:16–21. The Sea of Galilee, after dark.

The disciples are rowing across the lake in the dark, in a strong wind. Jesus comes to them on the water.

When therefore they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and drawing near to the boat; and they were afraid. But he said to them, “It is I. Don’t be afraid.”

John 6:19–20
Saying tied to it
It is I In Greek this is egō eimi, ‘I am’ (6:20). It is one of the absolute ‘I am’ sayings.
Old Testament background
God’s mastery of the sea: Your way was through the sea, your paths through the great waters (Psalm 77:19). ‘Do not be afraid’ is also the language God uses in Isaiah.
What it says about Jesus
He does what the Old Testament says God does, and he names himself with God’s own words as he does it.
Response
Fear, and then welcome: they were willing therefore to receive him into the boat.
6

The healing of the man born blind

John 9:1–41. Jerusalem, on a Sabbath, after the Festival of Tabernacles.

Jesus has already said, in the Temple at Tabernacles, that he is the light of the world. Now he says it again and acts it out. A man who has never seen is given sight.

Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.”

John 8:12

“While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” When he had said this, he spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, anointed the blind man’s eyes with the mud, and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So he went away, washed, and came back seeing.

John 9:5–7

Sight and blindness change places

The man moves step by step from sight to faith. The Pharisees, who are sure they can see, end the chapter blind.

Jesus said, “I came into this world for judgement, that those who don’t see may see; and that those who see may become blind.”

John 9:39
Saying tied to it
I am the light of the world 8:12; 9:5. The sign shows the saying.
Festival
At Tabernacles four great lamps were lit in the Court of Women to recall the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness.
Old Testament background
Creation: Let there be light (Genesis 1:3). The pillar of fire (Exodus 13:21). The LORD is my light and my salvation (Psalm 27:1). The servant as a light to the nations (Isaiah 49:6). The Dead Sea Scrolls also speak of ‘sons of light’.
What it says about Jesus
  • Revelation. Light lets people see the truth about God. Jesus makes the unseen God known (1:18).
  • Judgement. Light exposes. Belief and unbelief are the two responses (9:39–41).
  • For everyone. He is light of the world, not of Israel only (1:9).
  • Discipleship. He who follows me: light has to be walked in.
  • Replacement. Jesus fulfils the festival lamps.
Response
The man is thrown out of the synagogue (9:34). Jesus goes and finds him (9:35).
C D

The door and the good shepherd

John 10:1–21. Two sayings that follow straight from sign 6.

There is no new sign here. Chapter 10 comments on chapter 9. The Pharisees have thrown the healed man out. They are the thieves and hired hands who do not care for the sheep. Jesus went and found him.

I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved, and will go in and go out and will find pasture.

John 10:9

“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”

John 10:11

I am the good shepherd. I know my own, and I’m known by my own; even as the Father knows me, and I know the Father. I lay down my life for the sheep.

John 10:14–15
Old Testament background
God as shepherd: The LORD is my shepherd (Psalm 23:1); He will feed his flock like a shepherd (Isaiah 40:11). Ezekiel 34 condemns Israel’s leaders as shepherds who feed themselves. God promises: I myself, even I, will search for my sheep (34:11), and I will set up one shepherd over them … even my servant David (34:23).
What it says about Jesus
  • He does what God promised to do himself. This is an implied claim to divine identity.
  • His death is freely chosen. No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself (10:18). The cross is an act of love, not a defeat.
  • He knows his own. The shepherd knows the sheep even as the Father knows me. Believers are drawn into the relationship of Father and Son.
  • One flock. other sheep which are not of this fold (10:16): Gentiles are included.
  • The only way in. The door gives exclusive access to salvation (compare 14:6). The promise is still open: If anyone enters in by me.
Response
Division again (10:19–21). Some say, He has a demon and is insane!
Later
The theme returns at the Festival of Dedication (10:22–30): My sheep hear my voice, and I and the Father are one.
7

The raising of Lazarus

John 11:1–44. Bethany, near Jerusalem.

Lazarus has been dead four days. His sister Martha believes he will rise at the last day. Jesus answers that resurrection is a person, standing in front of her.

Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.”

John 11:24

Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”

John 11:25–26

When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Free him, and let him go.”

John 11:43–44
Saying tied to it
I am the resurrection and the life 11:25. The saying comes first. The sign then confirms it.
What it says about Jesus
  • He gives life as the Father does. 11:25 completes the claim of 5:21.
  • Resurrection is now and not yet. Eternal life begins with belief, which is realised eschatology. Physical death is still real: even if he dies. The last day is still to come (11:24).
  • It points ahead. The sign anticipates Jesus’ own resurrection. Lazarus returns to ordinary life and will die again, so he is a pointer to the resurrection, not the thing itself.
Response
Martha gives the confession the whole Gospel is written to produce: you are the Christ, God’s Son (11:27; compare 20:31). Others respond differently: from that day forward they took counsel that they might put him to death (11:53).
Why it is the climax
It is the last and greatest sign. It leads directly to the plot against Jesus, and so from the Book of Signs into the Book of Glory.
Exam note
The 2024 Edexcel mark scheme credited the point that the raising of Lazarus reaffirms the saying and anticipates Jesus’ resurrection.

Two sayings without a sign: the way and the vine

The last two sayings come in the Farewell Discourses, spoken to the disciples on the night before the crucifixion.

F

The way, the truth, and the life

John 14:6. Spoken to Thomas.

Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.”

John 14:6
What it says about Jesus
He is not a teacher who points to the way. He is the way. He also embodies truth (compare 1:14, 1:17 and Pilate’s question in 18:38).
Why it is debated
This is the most contested saying in modern theology because it is exclusive. John Hick challenged exclusive claims about Jesus in the name of religious pluralism.
G

The true vine

John 15:1–17. Spoken to the disciples only.

“I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer.”

John 15:1

I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.

John 15:5
Old Testament background
Israel as God’s vine: You brought a vine out of Egypt (Psalm 80:8). Isaiah’s song of the vineyard: the vineyard of the LORD of Armies is the house of Israel (Isaiah 5:7), and it gives only bad fruit. I had planted you a noble vine (Jeremiah 2:21). A golden vine decorated the entrance to the Temple, so the vine was a national symbol.
What it says about Jesus
  • He is the true Israel. Where Israel failed to bear fruit, Jesus is the true vine. Belonging to God’s people now means being joined to him, not to a nation.
  • Remain. The word ‘remain’ (menō) is repeated again and again. Eternal life is a relationship that has to be kept up.
  • Fruit and pruning. Discipleship means growth and discipline. Branches without fruit are cut off, so the saying is a warning as well as a promise.
  • The Father’s part. The Father tends the vine. The Son’s work is always the Father’s work.
Codes for living
The fruit is love, modelled on Jesus laying down his life. This is the clearest link between who Jesus is and how his followers should live.

“This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.”

John 15:12–13

‘I am’ on its own

The absolute sayings are the strongest claims of all. Each echoes the way God speaks in the Old Testament.

The absolute ‘I am’ sayings
WhereSayingSignificance
6:20It is I. Don’t be afraid.Walking on water. It echoes God’s mastery of the sea and the ‘do not fear’ language of Isaiah.
8:24unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sinsThe language of Isaiah 43:10.
8:28When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am heJesus’ identity is fully revealed at the cross.
8:58before Abraham came into existence, I AMPre-existence (compare 1:1). they took up stones to throw at him: they hear a claim to be God.
13:19that when it happens, you may believe that I am heForeknowledge, like God’s in Isaiah 41:4.
18:5–6When therefore he said to them, “I am he,” they went backward and fell to the groundAt the arrest the divine name overpowers the soldiers. Jesus is in control of his passion.

Big ideas and scholars

What the signs and sayings show, with the best evidence

Scholars to use
ScholarViewHow to use it
C H DoddThe sayings show Jesus as the one in whom eternal life is available now. Dodd explored Jewish backgrounds (Torah, Wisdom) and Hellenistic parallels, and argued that John spoke to both audiences. He described the pattern of sign followed by discourse.Use for eternal life and for the influence debate. Weakness: John also keeps future language (6:40; 14:3).
Raymond BrownDistinguished absolute sayings, sayings with an implied predicate, and predicated sayings. Read 6:51–58 as eucharistic. Stressed Jesus’ replacement of Jewish feasts and institutions.Use for the bread of life and for the festival settings.
C K BarrettStressed the Old Testament and Isaiah background of egō eimi, and Jesus’ divinity.Use for the absolute sayings.
Rudolf BultmannFound the ‘I am’ form in Gnostic and Hellenistic revelation speech. Doubted that the sayings were words of the historical Jesus.Use to challenge historicity. Weakness: the Dead Sea Scrolls show that much of the language is Jewish.
Geza VermesThe Jesus of the Synoptics never speaks like this. The sayings reflect the faith of the Johannine community.Use for AO2 on reliability. Counter: John may develop what was already implied in Jesus’ claims.

Debates to practise

Which reveals more: the sayings or the signs?

The case for the sayings

  • Jesus reveals himself in his own voice, using God’s way of speaking. The Prologue is the narrator’s voice, and Thomas’s confession is a disciple’s.
  • The sayings explain what the identity means, through Old Testament images he fulfils.
  • The 2024 Edexcel mark scheme described the sayings as a ‘direct theophany’, arguably more useful than the signs for understanding his ministry.

The case for the signs

  • The Gospel says the signs revealed his glory (2:11), and it names the signs, not the sayings, when it explains why it was written (20:30–31).
  • Signs are public and visible. Words can be dismissed, and are (10:20).
  • The raising of Lazarus provokes the plot to kill Jesus (11:53). The signs drive the story to the cross.

A way to judge between them: John shows again and again that signs are misread without interpretation. The crowd who ate the loaves want more bread (6:26). The Pharisees who see the blind man healed stay blind (9:41). Following Dodd, the saying is the key and the sign is its illustration. Both point on to the cross: When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he (8:28).

Are the ‘I am’ sayings the words of the historical Jesus?

Reasons to think they go back to Jesus

  • The Dead Sea Scrolls show that John’s language of light and darkness was already Jewish and first-century. That weakens the claim that it must come from later Greek or Gnostic sources.
  • Dodd and Robinson argue that John preserves independent historical tradition.
  • John may be developing what was already implied in Jesus’ own claims.

Reasons for doubt

  • Vermes: the Jesus of the Synoptics never speaks in this way.
  • Bultmann: the closest parallels to the ‘I am’ form are in Hellenistic and Gnostic revelation speech.
  • On this view the sayings show what the Johannine community came to believe about Jesus.

Read the question carefully. If it asks how the Fourth Gospel reveals who Jesus is, the historical objection changes the subject. Inside John’s narrative the sayings are still the main vehicle.

Religious laws and codes for living

  • Religious law. Two signs are done on the Sabbath. They raise the question of who has authority over the Law and what it is for.
  • Love. Bearing fruit means love, modelled on Jesus’ self-giving (15:12–13).
  • Leadership. The good shepherd is set against hired hands who do not care for the sheep. This is a challenge to religious authority.
  • Who belongs. Access is exclusive (10:9; 14:6), yet the invitation is to ‘whoever’ and reaches other sheep.
  • Following. Light has to be walked in (8:12). Believing is a way of living.

Questions to try

Written in Edexcel style. These are not past-paper questions.

  5. Analyse the significance of ‘I am the true vine’ for Christian codes for living.20 marks, AO1 and AO2
  6. Evaluate the view that the raising of Lazarus is the most important of the signs in the Fourth Gospel.30 marks, AO1 and AO2
  7. Evaluate the view that the ‘I am’ sayings are the most important way in which the Fourth Gospel reveals the identity of Jesus.30 marks, AO1 and AO2
  8. Evaluate the claim that the ‘I am’ sayings cannot be the words of the historical Jesus.30 marks, AO1 and AO2

  • explain egō eimi and its background in Exodus and Isaiah?
