The theology of John

John has the highest Christology of the four Gospels, and he teaches it through symbols that mean more than they first appear to. This room explains both, and then follows them into the cross, eternal life and the Spirit.

  • On this page
  • High Christology
  • The Son and the Father
  • John and the Synoptics
  • Deeper symbolism
  • The cross as glory
  • Eternal life
  • Spirit and community
  • Debates
  • Questions

Where this fits in the specification

  • Topics 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 all ask about the identity and role of Jesus. This room gathers what the Prologue, the sayings and the signs say into one picture.
  • Topic 3.2 lists John as a Spiritual Gospel among its purposes. The section on symbolism shows what that means in practice.
  • Each topic also asks about the implications for religious laws and codes for living.

High Christology

A high Christology starts from Jesus’ divine identity. John does this from his first sentence. The Gospel is framed by two statements that Jesus is God, one at each end.

The opening (1:1)

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

Spoken by the narrator, before the story begins.

Between the two: who Jesus is shown to be

  • The Word made flesh, who makes God known (1:14, 18)
  • The only Son, sent by the Father (3:16)
  • The Messiah, the King of Israel (1:41; 12:13)
  • The Son of Man who is lifted up (3:14; 12:32)
  • The one who says ‘I am’ (8:58)
  • One with the Father (10:30)

The climax (20:28)

My Lord and my God!

Spoken by Thomas, to the risen Jesus.

Everything between the two pillars fills in what they mean. John does not set one title against another. He uses more titles for Jesus than any other evangelist, and he piles them up.

How John names Jesus
Title or ideaKey versesWhat it says
The Word (Logos)1:1–3, 14Jesus is the eternal Word who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made. The idea draws on Jewish Wisdom and on Greek philosophy, so Jews and Gentiles could both follow it.
Son of God, the only Son1:14, 18; 3:16, 18Jesus is uniquely the ‘only’ Son (monogenēs). Believers are called ‘children’ of God. The Son acts with all the Father’s authority and depends on him completely.
Messiah1:41; 4:25–26; 9:22; 11:27; 20:31John is the only Gospel to use the Semitic word ‘Messiah’. The title runs through the whole book. Confessing it gets people put out of the synagogue. Jesus is the messianic king, though of a far higher kind than expected.
Son of Man1:51; 3:13–14; 5:27; 8:28; 12:32–34Linked with three things: judgement, being ‘lifted up’ in death and glory, and joining heaven and earth.
The prophet6:14 (Deuteronomy 18:15)The crowd see the prophet like Moses. John treats this as true but not enough: Jesus is God’s final and unique agent.
‘I am’8:24, 28, 58The absolute sayings echo the divine name of Exodus 3:14. Jesus claims a share in God’s eternal being.
God’s agent5:19–30; 12:45; 20:21Jesus is the one ‘sent’. Against the Jewish idea of agency, to meet the one sent is to meet the sender.

Four verses to know by heart

The Word became flesh and lived amongst us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.

John 1:14

No one has seen God at any time. The only born Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him.

John 1:18

“I and the Father are one.”

John 10:30

He who has seen me has seen the Father.

John 14:9

In 1:18 the NIV in your anthology adds that the Son ‘is himself God’.

The Son and the Father

John holds two things together. The Son is one with the Father. The Son also does nothing on his own. Both are said in the same chapters, often in the same breath.

Two sides of one relationship
One with the FatherSent by the Father and dependent on him
I and the Father are one. (10:30)the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing (5:19)
He who sees me sees him who sent me. (12:45)I do nothing of myself, but as my Father taught me, I say these things (8:28)
The Son gives life and judges, as God does (5:21–22).The Father has given all judgement to the Son (5:22). The authority is received.

The idea of agency explains how both can be true. In Jewish law an agent, a shaliach, carried the full authority of the one who sent him. Jesus is God’s unique agent. He judges, raises the dead and works on the Sabbath, which Jewish thought kept for God alone. So to meet Jesus is to meet God. After the resurrection the pattern is passed on:

Jesus therefore said to them again, “Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.”

John 20:21

Key points: who Jesus is in John

  • The Gospel is framed by 1:1 and 20:28.
  • The controlling idea is the Son: sent by the Father, one with the Father, obedient to the Father.
  • John keeps the title Messiah and redefines it. Jesus is the Christ and the Son of God (20:31).
  • In the incarnate Word, people are faced with God himself.

How John differs from the Synoptic Gospels

The same Jesus, told differently
FeatureSynoptic GospelsJohn
Jesus’ identityIn Mark, Jesus silences those who name him until after the resurrection. Scholars call this the messianic secret.Jesus makes ‘I am’ claims found in no other Gospel. People still fail to grasp them without faith.
The title ChristMostly confined to the passion story, and to the birth stories in Matthew and Luke.Appears throughout the book.
Speaking of his deathThree predictions that the Son of Man must suffer.Three sayings that the Son of Man must be ‘lifted up’ (3:14; 8:28; 12:32). The passion is exaltation.
GloryThe resurrection vindicates Jesus after his suffering.His whole life and ministry reveal glory, from the first sign (2:11). The resurrection is its final moment.
The disciplesIn Mark they have hardened hearts and often misunderstand.They believe because they see his glory (2:11).
Miracles‘Mighty deeds’, including exorcisms.Seven signs. No exorcisms.
TeachingParables. In Mark the kingdom of God is the theme of Jesus’ preaching.Long discourses. No parables. Salvation is described as eternal life and new birth.

Deeper symbolism: reading John on two levels

Clement of Alexandria called John a ‘spiritual Gospel’. One reason is the way John writes. People, places, objects and even the time of day carry a second meaning. Characters in the story usually hear only the surface. The reader, who has read the Prologue, is meant to hear both.

Five techniques to spot

1. Symbols from the Old Testament

Bread, light, shepherd and vine were already pictures of God’s gifts or of Israel. John has Jesus claim each one. A sign works the same way: the event is real, and it points beyond itself.

Example: water kept for purification becomes wine (2:6–11). The old order gives way to the messianic age.

2. Dualism

John sets pairs against each other: light and darkness, above and below, flesh and spirit, sight and blindness. This dualism is close to the language of the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Example: night. Nicodemus came to Jesus by night (3:2). When Judas leaves the supper, It was night (13:30). Mary comes to the tomb while it was still dark (20:1).

3. Misunderstanding

Someone takes Jesus’ words literally. The mistake gives Jesus, or the narrator, the chance to explain.

Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The Jews therefore said, “It took forty-six years to build this temple! Will you raise it up in three days?” But he spoke of the temple of his body.

John 2:19–21

4. Words with two meanings

‘Lifted up’ means raised on a cross and raised in glory. John tells the reader so.

“And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die.

John 12:32–33

5. Irony

With irony, opponents say what is true without knowing it. Pilate writes a mocking title and refuses to change it.

Pilate wrote a title also, and put it on the cross. There was written, “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”

John 19:19

The chief priests reply, We have no king but Caesar! (19:15). Pilate asks, What is truth? (18:38) of the one who has said I am the way, the truth, and the life.

How a symbol works

For Paul Tillich a symbol takes part in the reality it points to and opens up understanding of it. On that account bread, light and vine are not decoration. They are how John reveals who Jesus is.

A J Ayer’s verification principle would say that ‘I am the bread of life’ is not a factual claim at all. This links John to your work on religious language.

Surface meaning and deeper meaning
WhereWhat is saidWhat the hearer thinksWhat John means
2:19–21Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.The building in Jerusalem, forty-six years in the making.the temple of his body: his death and resurrection.
3:3–6unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s KingdomNicodemus: How can a man be born when he is old?A new birth from God: That which is born of the Spirit is spirit.
6:26–35Bread from heaven.The crowd: Lord, always give us this bread.I am the bread of life. Jesus himself is the gift.
9:39–41Sight and blindness.The Pharisees: Are we also blind?To see is to believe. To be sure you see, and reject him, is blindness.
12:32–34The Son of Man must be lifted up.The crowd: the Christ is supposed to remain for ever.The cross is his exaltation.
18:33–37Are you the King of the Jews?Pilate: a political rival to Caesar.My Kingdom is not of this world. He is a king who testifies to the truth.

Does symbolism make John less historical?

Strengths of reading John symbolically

  • It follows the text. John often explains the second meaning himself (2:21; 12:33).
  • It explains why John chose only seven signs and attached discourses to them.
  • It fits Clement’s early description of John as a ‘spiritual Gospel’.

Weaknesses and limits

  • It can be taken to mean John did not care about facts. Dodd and Robinson argue that he preserves independent historical tradition.
  • The Gospel insists that the Word became flesh (1:14) and rests on eyewitness testimony (19:35). A reading that dissolves events into ideas drifts towards Docetism.
  • Readers can find symbols John never intended.

The cross as glory

In John the death of Jesus is not a defeat that the resurrection puts right. It is the moment his glory is shown. Glory and death are almost the same thing: the cross is at once his lifting up to the Father and the completion of his work.

As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.

John 3:14–15

Jesus answered them, “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.”

John 12:23

Father, the time has come. Glorify your Son, that your Son may also glorify you

John 17:1
  • He is in control. At the arrest he says I am he and the soldiers fall to the ground (18:5–6). He lays his life down himself (10:18).
  • He is king. The trial before Pilate turns on kingship. The charge on the cross tells the truth (19:19–22).
  • He returns to where he began. He asks for the glory which I had with you before the world existed (17:5). This takes us back to 1:1.
  • The resurrection completes it. It is the last moment in the drama of glory, and it leads to Thomas’s confession.

Salvation and eternal life

John sums up salvation in one sentence.

This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.

John 17:3

Eternal life is the life God himself has, given through the Son to all who believe. What marks John out is that this life is already possessed.

“Most certainly I tell you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgement, but has passed out of death into life.”

John 5:24

Eschatology is teaching about the last things. Dodd called John’s emphasis on the present realised eschatology. John does not give up the future, though. The two stand side by side.

Already and not yet
AlreadyNot yet
The believer has passed out of death into life (5:24).the hour comes in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice (5:28).
he who believes in me has eternal life (6:47).I will raise him up at the last day (6:40).
I am the resurrection and the life (11:25).he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day (11:24).

New birth

Salvation is also described as being born anew. Ethnic descent and ritual do not bring a person into God’s people. A new work of the Spirit does.

Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and Spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom. That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit.”

John 3:5–6

This is what the Prologue promised: those who believe are given the right to become God’s children (1:12).

The Spirit and the community

In the Farewell Discourses Jesus promises that when he goes he will send the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, to continue his work. The translation used here calls him the Counsellor.

I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counsellor, that he may be with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive, for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him. You know him, for he lives with you and will be in you.

John 14:16–17
What the Paraclete does
RoleVerse
Teacherwill teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you (14:26)
Witnesshe will testify about me (15:26)
Guide into truthhe will guide you into all truth (16:13)
Accuser of the world16:8–11

The community gathered around the Spirit is marked by unity, modelled on the Father and the Son (that they may be one, even as we are, 17:11), and by self-giving love (15:12–17). Its calling is to bear witness to the truth. On Easter evening Jesus gives the Spirit:

When he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit!”

John 20:22

Debates to practise

Is John’s high Christology a late invention?

Reasons to think it is early and rooted in Judaism

  • The Rylands Papyrus P52 shows the Gospel existed by about the end of the first century.
  • The Dead Sea Scrolls show that its language was at home in first-century Palestinian Judaism (Brown).
  • Its key ideas are Jewish: Wisdom, the Word, the divine name, the agent who is sent.
  • Robinson argues that John is an early and independent witness.

Reasons to think it is a later development

  • The Jesus of the Synoptics does not speak this way (Vermes).
  • Most scholars date John to about 90–100 CE, after decades of reflection.
  • Brown’s community model has the Gospel growing in stages, shaped by conflict with the synagogue.

A caution from the scholarship: it would be wrong to read the later ‘two natures’ doctrine back into the Gospel. Yet only a shallow reading could miss how exalted John’s view of Jesus is.

‘My Lord and my God’: what is Thomas saying?

It is the climax of the Gospel’s Christology

  • It matches the Prologue’s claim (1:1, 14) and so frames the Gospel.
  • It goes beyond saying that Jesus is alive. It says what his resurrection means: he is one with the Father.
  • The purpose statement follows at once (20:30–31).

It is only a devout exclamation

  • On this reading Thomas is crying out in amazement, not making a statement about Jesus’ nature.
  • This reading is hard to keep up, because the words are addressed to Jesus: Thomas answered him.

Is Jesus the only way?

The exclusive reading

  • No one comes to the Father, except through me. (14:6). The door saying says the same (10:9).
  • The claim is framed by the divine name. If Jesus is who John says he is, the claim follows.
  • The invitation is universal: light for the world, life for whoever believes.

The pluralist challenge

  • John Hick argues that such claims are the love-language of a community, not literal metaphysics.
  • On that view the sayings express devotion and should not be used to judge other religions.
  • Reply: Hick’s reading rests on his prior commitment to pluralism more than on the text.

Reading ‘the Jews’ in John with care

John often sets ‘the Jews’ as a group over against those who believe in Jesus. This reflects tension between church and synagogue at the time the Gospel took shape (9:22). The Gospel’s own background is deeply Jewish, as the Dead Sea Scrolls confirm.

The idea that Jesus replaces Jewish institutions has sometimes fed hostility towards Judaism. Many modern scholars stress that John also presents the Law as a real gift (1:16–17). Say this when you use the term replacement theology.

Religious laws and codes for living

  • Authority. If Jesus is the Word made flesh, his teaching carries God’s authority, above the Law given through Moses (1:17).
  • Love. The one command he gives his followers is love modelled on his own death (15:12–13).
  • Belonging. People become God’s children by belief and new birth, not by descent or ritual (1:12–13; 3:5–6).
  • Witness. The community is sent as Jesus was sent (20:21).
  • Other faiths. The exclusive sayings raise the question of pluralism.

Questions to try

Written in Edexcel style. These are not past-paper questions.

  1. Explore what the Fourth Gospel means by calling Jesus the Son of God.8 marks, AO1
  2. Explore the ways in which the Fourth Gospel uses symbolism to show who Jesus is.8 marks, AO1
  3. Assess the view that in the Fourth Gospel the cross is a moment of glory, not of defeat.12 marks, AO1 and AO2
  4. Assess the claim that eternal life in the Fourth Gospel is entirely a present reality.12 marks, AO1 and AO2
  5. Evaluate the view that the Fourth Gospel presents Jesus as God.30 marks, AO1 and AO2
  6. Evaluate the view that the symbolism of the Fourth Gospel makes it less reliable as an account of Jesus.30 marks, AO1 and AO2

Can I…?

  • explain what ‘high Christology’ means, with two verses?
  • explain how Jesus can be one with the Father and sent by the Father?
  • give three examples of words or events with two levels of meaning?
  • explain why John calls the cross glory?
  • explain realised eschatology and show that John keeps a future hope too?
  • describe the work of the Paraclete?

Glossary

Every technical term in the tour, in alphabetical order. Each entry lists the rooms where the word is used, and each link takes you to the place.

Absolute ‘I am’ saying

A saying in which Jesus says ‘I am’ with no noun after it. It is a claim about who he is, and it echoes God’s own name (for example John 8:58).

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Agency (shaliach)

A Jewish legal idea in which an authorised agent (a shaliach, ‘one who is sent’) acts with the full authority of the person who sent him. In John, Jesus is God’s unique agent, so to meet Jesus is to meet God.

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs, Theology

Anthology

The set of Bible extracts Edexcel publishes for this paper. An anthology passage may be printed on the exam paper, so you can quote from it and analyse it.

Used in Start, The Prologue, ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Beloved Disciple

The unnamed ‘disciple whom Jesus loved’ (John 13:23; 19:26; 20:2; 21:7, 20–24). Tradition identifies him with the apostle John, but most modern scholars treat his identity as uncertain. The Gospel presents him as the witness on whom its traditions rest.

Used in Author and purpose

Birkat ha-minim

A ‘benediction against heretics’ linked with the rabbinic council at Jamnia (about 85–90 CE). Some scholars think it explains John’s references to being put out of the synagogue (9:22; 12:42; 16:2). Its wording and date are still debated.

Used in Author and purpose

Book of Glory

The second main part of John (13:1–20:31): the Last Supper, the Farewell Discourses, and the passion and resurrection.

Used in Start, ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Book of Signs

C H Dodd’s name for the first main part of John (1:19–12:50), which narrates all the signs and sets them against the Jewish festivals.

Used in Start, ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Chiasm

A mirror-shaped structure (A–B–C–B–A) in which the most important point sits in the centre.

Used in The Prologue

Christology

The study of who Jesus is and how he relates to God.

Used in The Prologue, Theology

Dead Sea Scrolls

Jewish texts found near Qumran, by the Dead Sea, from 1947 onwards. Most scholars identify them as the library of the Essene community.

Used in The Prologue

Dedication (Hanukkah)

A Jewish festival. John sets Jesus’ words ‘I and the Father are one’ at this feast (10:22–30).

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Diaspora

Jewish communities living outside Palestine, spread across the ancient world.

Used in Author and purpose

Docetism

An early belief (from the Greek dokeō, ‘to seem’) that Jesus only seemed to have a human body and did not truly suffer.

Used in Author and purpose, The Prologue, Theology

Dualism

A view of reality as two opposing forces, for example light and darkness.

Used in The Prologue, Theology

Egō eimi

Greek for ‘I am’. It is ordinary Greek, but in the Septuagint it is how God speaks of himself (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:10).

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Eschatology

Teaching about the ‘last things’: final judgement, resurrection and eternal life.

Used in Theology

Essenes

A small and very strict Jewish party of about 4,000 members, described by Josephus and Philo. Most scholars link them with the Qumran community and the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Used in The Prologue

Eternal life (zōē aiōnios)

Literally ‘life of the age to come’: the life God himself has, given through the Son to all who believe. In John it begins in the present (5:24; 17:3).

Used in The Prologue, Theology

Eucharist

The Christian meal of bread and wine that recalls Jesus’ death, also called the Lord’s Supper.

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Evangelist

The author of a Gospel. The term stresses that the Gospel writers were theological authors, not only reporters.

Used in Theology

Farewell Discourses

Jesus’ private teaching to his disciples on the night of his arrest (John 14–17, within the Last Supper scene that begins in chapter 13). The material is found only in John.

Used in Start, ‘I am’ sayings and signs, Theology

Fourth Gospel

A common scholarly name for the Gospel of John, which sets it apart from the three Synoptic Gospels.

Used in Author and purpose

Gentiles

Non-Jewish peoples.

Used in Author and purpose

Glory (doxa)

God’s splendour and presence made visible. In John, Jesus’ whole ministry reveals glory (2:11), and his death is the hour when he is glorified (12:23; 17:1–5).

Used in The Prologue, Theology

Gnosticism

Movements teaching that salvation comes through secret knowledge and that matter is inferior or evil.

Used in The Prologue

Hellenism

The spread of Greek language and culture after Alexander the Great (died 323 BCE).

Used in The Prologue

High Christology

An account of Jesus that stresses his divine identity: he existed before creation and shares the nature of God. John has the highest Christology of the four Gospels (1:1; 20:28).

Used in Theology

Incarnation

God becoming human (‘in flesh’). It is the claim of John 1:14.

Used in The Prologue

Irony

A way of writing in which the reader understands more than the characters do. In John, opponents often say something true about Jesus without knowing it.

Used in Theology

Johannine community

The group of early Christians among whom John’s Gospel is thought to have been written.

Used in Author and purpose, ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Logos

The Greek word translated ‘Word’. It can mean word, speech, reason or rational principle. The Prologue uses it for the eternal Word through whom all things were made.

Used in Author and purpose, The Prologue, Theology

Memra

Aramaic for ‘Word’. The Targums use it as a respectful way to speak of God acting in the world.

Used in The Prologue

Messiah (Christ)

‘Anointed one’: God’s anointed representative, expected by many as a king descended from David. ‘Messiah’ is the Semitic word and ‘Christ’ is its Greek translation.

Used in Author and purpose, Theology

Midrash

A Jewish method of interpreting and expanding Scripture.

Used in The Prologue

Monogenēs

A Greek word meaning ‘unique’ or ‘only’. John uses it for Jesus as the ‘only Son’ of the Father (1:14, 18; 3:16, 18).

Used in Theology

Paraclete

From the Greek paraklētos: a title for the Holy Spirit in John 14–16. Translations include ‘Advocate’, ‘Counsellor’, ‘Comforter’ and ‘Helper’.

Used in Theology

Passover

The Jewish festival that recalls the Exodus from Egypt. John sets the feeding of the five thousand near Passover (6:4).

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Personification

Describing an idea, such as Wisdom, as if it were a person.

Used in The Prologue

Pharisees

A largely lay Jewish party of about 6,000 members, known for precise interpretation of the Law.

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Philo of Alexandria

A Jewish philosopher (about 20 BCE to about 50 CE) who used Greek ideas to explain the Jewish Scriptures. He described the Logos as God’s intermediary in creation.

Used in Author and purpose, The Prologue

Predicated ‘I am’ saying

A saying in which ‘I am’ is completed by a noun (the predicate), such as bread, light or vine. The image explains what Jesus does for people.

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Pre-existence

The belief that the Word existed before creation (John 1:1–2).

Used in The Prologue, ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Prologue

The opening of John’s Gospel (1:1–18).

Used in Author and purpose, Theology

Qumran

A site near the Dead Sea. Most scholars link the community that lived there with the Essenes and with the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Used in The Prologue

Realised eschatology

C H Dodd’s term for the view that the ‘last things’, such as eternal life and judgement, are already present in Jesus.

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs, Theology

Replacement theology

Here, the idea that Jesus fulfils and replaces Jewish institutions such as the Temple, the Law and the festivals.

Used in The Prologue, ‘I am’ sayings and signs, Theology

Rylands Papyrus P52

A small papyrus fragment of John 18:31–33, 37–38 from Egypt, dated to the early second century. It is the oldest known manuscript of the New Testament. It shows that John must have been written by the end of the first century, or the very early second century at the latest.

Used in Author and purpose, Theology

Sabbath

The seventh day of the week, on which work was forbidden.

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Septuagint (LXX)

The Greek translation of the Old Testament used by Greek-speaking Jews and early Christians.

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Shekinah

God’s glorious presence dwelling among his people, as when the glory filled the Tabernacle (Exodus 40:34).

Used in The Prologue

Sign (sēmeion)

John’s word for a miracle. A sign is a revealing act that points beyond itself to who Jesus is.

Used in Start, ‘I am’ sayings and signs, Theology

Son of Man

A title Jesus uses of himself. In John it is linked with his being ‘lifted up’, with judgement, and with his role joining heaven and earth (1:51).

Used in Theology

Sophia

Greek for ‘wisdom’.

Used in The Prologue

Staircase parallelism

A poetic pattern in which the last key word of one line becomes the first key word of the next.

Used in The Prologue

Stoics

Philosophers who taught that the Logos is divine reason running through all things, and that every person shares a seed of it.

Used in The Prologue

Symbol

Something that points beyond itself. For Paul Tillich a symbol also takes part in the reality it points to.

Used in Theology

Synagogue

A local Jewish meeting place where people gathered on the Sabbath to study the Law and pray.

Used in Author and purpose

Synoptic Gospels

Matthew, Mark and Luke. They can be ‘seen together’ because they share a common outline, many of the same stories and much of the same wording.

Used in Author and purpose

Tabernacle

The tent of God’s presence that Israel carried through the wilderness.

Used in The Prologue

Tabernacles (Sukkot)

A Jewish festival, also called the Feast of Booths. Great lamps were lit in the Temple to recall the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness.

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Targum

An Aramaic paraphrase of Scripture read in synagogues.

Used in The Prologue

Terminus ante quem

Latin for ‘limit before which’: the latest possible date by which a document must have been written.

Used in Author and purpose

Theophany

An appearance or self-revelation of God.

Used in ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Torah

The Law revealed to Moses on Sinai: the first five books of the Bible.

Used in The Prologue, ‘I am’ sayings and signs

Wisdom literature

Books such as Proverbs and Job, with Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon in the Apocrypha. In them Wisdom is pictured as a female figure who was with God at creation.

Used in The Prologue
